stories.topic: The Economist Who Puked on a Forest
stories.summary: During a few days in Bir, Ajay spent time with trail runner Sanat Sachdev, who got him thinking about running in the mountains. He also took a two-hour tandem paragliding ride. At the highest point the air turned rocky, and his pilot calmly taught him how to stick his head out and throw up onto the forest below. Amit wondered whether he was the first economist ever to do so.
stories.insight: A warm, self-deprecating opener that sets the show's tone. Ajay shrugs it off by noting that anyone who paraglides seriously deals with motion sickness. Discomfort is simply part of the adventure.
stories.quote: the guy behind me, the pilot, gently instructed me on how to stick my head out and puke on the forest below.

stories.topic: When You Could Rent a Bombay Flat in Fifteen Minutes
stories.summary: Around 1976, when Ajay was about ten, his father told the family over dinner what Bombay was like when he arrived in 1942, the year Gandhiji launched the Quit India movement. Back then you could walk the streets and rent a flat within fifteen minutes. By the 1970s, rent control and the pagdi system had made renting nearly impossible, so the children listened wide-eyed to what sounded like a fairy tale.
stories.insight: Rent control's deepest damage is invisible to anyone born after it arrives. A whole generation grew up thinking a broken housing market was normal, when a free rental market had once worked effortlessly in the same city.
stories.quote: When I first came to Bombay, you could just walk around the street and within fifteen minutes you could rent a flat.

stories.topic: Hitler's Autobahns and the Great Depression Exception
stories.summary: Ajay broadly agrees with Hazlitt on make-work spending but offers one exception: the Great Depression. Monetary mistakes collapsed the money supply and roughly a quarter of banks failed. Because banks held unique information about their borrowers, firms that lost their bank could not easily start over with a new one. Hitler then borrowed to fund rearmament and the autobahns, which he actually wanted, and the resulting jobs and re-spending pulled Germany out of the Depression. Roosevelt's Tennessee Valley Authority had similar effects. Amit pushed back, pointing to contrary accounts by Amity Shlaes and Thomas Sowell.
stories.insight: Economic rules come with context. Ajay sees debt-financed stimulus as defensible only when the financial system has collapsed, and argues that modern policy would never repeat the mistakes that caused that collapse. Hosts who agree on fundamentals still disagree on edge cases.
stories.quote: He actually wanted the arms, he actually wanted the autobahns. So it's not as if he was doing it for the purpose of solving the economic problems of the country.

stories.topic: The Bureaucrat Who Wanted to Save Jute
stories.summary: Amit once asked a senior West Bengal bureaucrat who looked after the jute industry what the thinking was. The answer: jute is struggling, it is an indigenous industry, it is 'our thing', so the government must keep it alive with subsidies, price controls and land grants. Amit asked why the government had any role at all, and argued that supply and demand should decide. Ajay later added a twist: jute today is doing extremely well, because global technological forces made the world want more of it, and this has nothing to do with the government.
stories.insight: This is Hazlitt's 'Saving the X Industry' in real life. Any subsidy to one industry is taken from others whose lost jobs and welfare go unseen. The punchline is that the industry thrived without being 'saved'.
stories.quote: And I was like, Why? Why does the government have a role to play in it?

stories.summary: About twenty years ago, Barun Mitra was part of a movement to win property rights for tribals in Gujarat. Using historical Google Earth satellite imagery, they proved how long the tribals had lived on the land and where its boundaries lay, and the tribals got their titles. The first thing the tribals did was build pakka houses and toilets, which they had never done while they could be evicted at any time. The story is told in the documentary India Awakes.
stories.insight: Ownership changes incentives overnight. People do not invest in land they could lose, and once it is theirs, they build. This is Hernando de Soto's 'dead capital' coming back to life.
stories.quote: And the first thing they did, when they got the rights, was made pakka housing for themselves. They built toilets for themselves.

stories.topic: The Leftist Friend Surprised That Amit Cared
stories.summary: A few years ago an ardent leftist friend told Amit, mid-conversation, that he hadn't realised Amit cared so much, because he assumed libertarians don't care about people. Amit recalled this on reading a Daniel Hannan tweet arguing that the left's defining trait is not compassion but the conviction that compassion belongs only to their side.
stories.insight: Disagreement about policy is often mistaken for disagreement about values. Critics of rent control or price controls usually care about the same people, and they ask whether the policy actually helps them.
stories.quote: Amit, I didn't realise you cared so much. I thought you're libertarian, you don't give a shit about people.

stories.summary: After invoking Arthur C. Clarke on technology and magic, Amit showed Ajay a painting by the artist Tatsuo Horiuchi and quizzed him on the medium. Ajay had no idea. It was made in Microsoft Excel, the same spreadsheet technology Ajay had just described as still not fully adopted across Indian business, decades after it arrived.
stories.insight: Tools spread slowly, and in the right hands they are used in ways no one planned. A spreadsheet becomes a paintbrush.
stories.quote: He made it using a technology you referred to five minutes ago. He made it using Microsoft Excel.

recommendations.item: Economics in One Lesson
recommendations.creator: Henry Hazlitt
recommendations.context: The book this whole episode breaks down. It is the first in a new series where every five episodes or so the hosts pick a book that shaped them.
recommendations.reason: It is a 1946 'collection of light bulbs' on economic fallacies that are still committed today. Hazlitt never changed a word of the original text in later editions because the principles still held. Lant Pritchett told Amit it turned him onto economics, and one of Ajay's mentees says the same. Ajay urges listeners to read the book itself rather than treat the episode as a substitute.

recommendations.item: Basic Economics
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Named alongside Hazlitt as one of the few true primers on economics.
recommendations.reason: Along with Sowell's other books, it is one of Amit's go-to answers when asked for a single fundamental book on the subject.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited as an example of a rare foundational primer in a field that lacks one.
recommendations.reason: There are very few primers on public policy, and fewer still that place it in the Indian context. This book does both, which is why it matters so much to Amit.

recommendations.item: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Ep 45 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced when explaining why Hazlitt's fallacies keep recurring.
recommendations.reason: It explains why economics' deepest truths, such as spontaneous order and positive-sum exchange, are counterintuitive, and why intuition pulls us towards zero-sum, top-down thinking.

recommendations.item: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Ep 46 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Listed among past episodes that echo Hazlitt's themes.
recommendations.reason: Amit says luxury beliefs are full of the same kinds of fallacies Hazlitt dissects.

recommendations.item: Don't Mess With the Price System (Ep 66 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Pointed to instead of repeating the case against price controls here.
recommendations.reason: It covers the near-law that price controls always lead to shortages, and why the price system should be treated as sacred.

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Ep 379 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Mentioned twice: Pritchett said Hazlitt turned him onto economics, and they discussed growth versus redistribution.
recommendations.reason: A deep conversation on why growth, not redistribution, drives human welfare.

recommendations.item: Economic growth is enough and only economic growth is enough
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Cited in the growth-versus-redistribution discussion.
recommendations.reason: Pritchett finds that a wide range of human welfare indicators, from health onwards, correlate at around 99% with per capita GDP. That leaves redistribution and welfarism a sliver of the story.

recommendations.item: Four Papers That Changed the World (Ep 41 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled while describing the light-bulb moments that retrain intuition.
recommendations.reason: It includes Hayek's essay on prices, which gave Amit his light-bulb moment about how prices work.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Named as one of Amit's own light bulbs.
recommendations.reason: Understanding how prices carry knowledge made the folly and hubris of legislating prices impossible to unsee.

recommendations.item: The Evolution of Everything
recommendations.creator: Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Cited for showing spontaneous order everywhere.
recommendations.reason: It made Amit see spontaneous order running through natural selection, the evolution of language, prices and all of society. He calls it 'so miraculous'.

recommendations.item: The Evolution of Everything (Ep 96 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Amit's conversation with Ridley about the book.
recommendations.reason: A companion to the book on how bottom-up order shapes the world.

recommendations.item: That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen
recommendations.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.context: The mid-19th-century essay that inspired both Hazlitt's book and the name of Amit's podcast.
recommendations.reason: Its parable of the broken window is the cleanest illustration of looking past the visible effect to the unseen opportunity cost.

recommendations.item: How to Do Development (Ep 57 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Raised by Ajay in the growth-versus-redistribution discussion. Amit urged listeners to watch it.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it profoundly important: sustained growth, not class-warfare redistribution, is what makes people better off.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Ep 25 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced in the chapter on public works.
recommendations.reason: It makes the point that nothing the government does is free. Everything is paid for through taxes, and therefore through coercion.

recommendations.item: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Ep 55 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's caution against exuberance about public works.
recommendations.reason: It challenges India's optimism about every new road and airport. Infrastructure has diminishing returns, roads can lead nowhere, and many outcomes expected from the 1990s build-out never arrived.

recommendations.item: The Forgotten Man: A New History of the Great Depression
recommendations.creator: Amity Shlaes
recommendations.context: Amit's counterpoint to Ajay's view that Depression-era spending pulled economies out.
recommendations.reason: It offers the contrary reading of the Depression that Amit has a lot of sympathy for.

recommendations.item: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Ep 59 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Brought up after Amit called the space program a waste of money.
recommendations.reason: The episode where the hosts debated state projects like the space program.

recommendations.item: Who Lends to the Indian State?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah & co-authors
recommendations.context: Cited in the chapter on government credit.
recommendations.reason: XKDR Forum's paper is the first to measure India's financial repression. Its headline finding is that 95% of the Indian state's borrowing is coerced out of the financial system.

recommendations.item: The Globalisation Episode (Ep 95 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Pointed to for Hazlitt's chapters on tariffs.
recommendations.reason: It makes the case that tariffs always harm your own people and redistribute wealth from the poor to the rich.

recommendations.item: Is Globalization Doomed? (Ep 96 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The second of the two globalisation episodes Amit points to on tariffs.
recommendations.reason: It continues the discussion of trade and tariffs.

recommendations.item: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: One of the hosts' columns linked instead of re-arguing price controls.
recommendations.reason: It explains why price controls always cause scarcities and hurt the people they claim to protect.

recommendations.item: Prices, Fast and Slow
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Another of the hosts' linked columns on price controls.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's take on the same theme of what happens when the state messes with prices.

recommendations.item: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate (Ep 67 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned as an extension of the price-control argument.
recommendations.reason: The exchange rate is a price too, and controlling it causes the same distortions.

recommendations.item: Episode 14 of The Seen and the Unseen: Rent Control
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
recommendations.context: An early, roughly twenty-minute episode from when the show was very Bastiat-inspired.
recommendations.reason: A short primer on the unseen consequences of rent control, which is back in the news.

recommendations.item: The Mystery of Capital
recommendations.creator: Hernando de Soto
recommendations.context: Introduced as a 'great concept' during the rent control discussion.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it essential reading and a masterpiece. It explains 'dead capital': without property rights, slum dwellers and tribals cannot borrow against or invest in what they effectively own.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State
recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: Quoted on why property rights drive land improvement. Amit says a full episode on it is coming.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it an amazing book that the hosts have discussed many times. It contains his favourite line on ownership: 'the greatest fertilizer of all is the tender gaze of an owner'.

recommendations.item: Daniel Hannan's tweet on the left and compassion
recommendations.creator: Daniel Hannan
recommendations.context: A tweet Amit saw on the day of recording.
recommendations.reason: It argues that the left's defining trait is not compassion but the conviction that compassion is unique to their side, which leads to a grotesque misreading of the other side.

recommendations.item: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Suggested alongside Hazlitt's chapter on the minimum wage.
recommendations.reason: A great video on how minimum wages hurt the poor they are meant to help.

recommendations.item: India Awakes
recommendations.creator: Johan Norberg
recommendations.context: A documentary presented by Johan Norberg, produced via the Free to Choose network.
recommendations.reason: It tells Barun Mitra's story of using satellite imagery to win land rights for tribals.

recommendations.item: The early Seen and the Unseen episode on demonetisation with Suyash Rai
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
recommendations.context: Cited while explaining Hazlitt's tool of looking at general welfare.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of Suyash's point that cost-benefit analysis hides an immorality when costs fall on one group and benefits on another.

core_ideas.concept: The One Lesson: Look at Longer Effects and All Groups
core_ideas.explanation: Hazlitt's whole book in a sentence. The bad economist sees only the immediate, direct effect on one visible group. The good economist traces the longer, indirect effects on everyone. Policies that look compassionate at first glance often turn out to harm the very people they purport to help.
core_ideas.quote: The art of economics consists in looking not merely at the immediate but at the longer effects of any act or policy. It consists in tracing the consequences of that policy not merely for one group, but for all groups.

core_ideas.concept: The Broken Window and Opportunity Cost
core_ideas.explanation: From Bastiat's parable: a broken shop window looks like stimulus because the glazier gets paid. What goes unseen is the suit the shopkeeper would have bought with the same money, and the tailor who would have spent it. The same logic demolishes the claim that war, or rebuilding destroyed cities, is good for the economy.
core_ideas.quote: What is not seen is what the shopkeeper would have done with the twenty rupees had he kept it with himself.

core_ideas.explanation: Our default intuitions are zero-sum and top-down. Ideas like how prices work or spontaneous order switch on a light that can't be switched off, and they become our new intuition. Ajay says the price system and general equilibrium are now his 3 a.m. default, while market imperfections must be layered on consciously.
core_ideas.quote: But then you have what I call these light bulb moments that you flick a switch and the light comes on. And you can never unsee what you have just seen.

core_ideas.explanation: Sustained growth transforms everyone's life. Redistribution is the seen benefit with unseen costs: coercion, distorted incentives and slower growth. Lant Pritchett's work finds that welfare indicators correlate around 99% with per capita GDP. Ajay sees redistribution politics as divide-and-conquer.
core_ideas.quote: But so many people are willing to sacrifice growth and instead focus themselves on all the political harm that goes with redistribution. This is a game of class warfare.

core_ideas.explanation: Make-work projects show you the visible workers on the bridge but hide the private jobs that the taxes destroyed. Once employment becomes the goal, governments stop asking where bridges must be built and start asking where they can be built. Amit sees NREGS as a modern example with crowding-out effects.
core_ideas.quote: For every public job created by the bridge project, a private job has been destroyed somewhere else.

core_ideas.concept: Taxes Discourage Production, and Taxes as Time
core_ideas.explanation: Taxing Ajay to give to Amit is not a neutral transfer. It blunts Ajay's incentive to produce, expand and take risks. Translate tax into months worked for the state and it becomes visceral. Everyone pays tax, including the beggar buying salt and the domestic help buying soap, and inflation is a tax on the poor. Indira Gandhi's peak personal rate of roughly 95 to 97% pushed people to leave the country or hoard black money. Amit applies the same opportunity-cost lens to India's space program.
core_ideas.quote: If you are taxed one third of your income, that means that for four months of the year you are working for the government of India, you're not working for yourself. Taxation is part time slavery.

core_ideas.explanation: Finance means processing information, forecasting and taking risks, and it requires tolerating failures. Bureaucrats have no incentive to do this hard work, and government finance invites political capture. That capture takes the form of financial repression to fund the state, directed lending to agriculture, and pressure to favour particular borrowers.
core_ideas.quote: This entire spectrum of government intervention into finance is just a dismal mess.

core_ideas.explanation: Every era fears that technology will kill jobs, from the Luddites to the anti-automation voices of the 1960s to today's AI worriers. Hazlitt uses Adam Smith's pin makers to show that, by this logic, machinery should have caused near-total unemployment. Instead productivity gains spill into the economy and create jobs. If saving labour were bad, freight should be carried on men's backs.
core_ideas.quote: There's never been an exception, and there is no reason to believe there will be an exception this time.

core_ideas.concept: Production Equals Consumption, and Diffusion Is Slow
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's two-part rebuttal to technology panic. First, a society can only consume what it produces, so productivity gains are gains in per capita consumption. Second, adoption takes time: steam, electricity and spreadsheets all spread slowly, which leaves room to adjust. Driverless cars will replace India's drivers 'with probability one', but over perhaps 25 years, not overnight.
core_ideas.quote: The aggregate consumption of society is the aggregate production of society.

core_ideas.explanation: You can build an electric vehicle in Mahindra's Igatpuri factory, or you can raise chickens on Maharashtra's poultry farms, ship frozen chicken out of JNPT, and get EVs back. Both are technologies that turn inputs into outputs. Tariffs are therefore industrial policy that picks a winner between them. To stop progress you would have to shut down trade as well as science.
core_ideas.quote: So sitting at JNPT is a piece of magic that converts frozen chicken into electric vehicles. And that's a technology, and it's a very cool technology.

core_ideas.concept: Culture Decides Whether Change Becomes Conflict
core_ideas.explanation: Technological change always hurts some firms, creditors and workers. In a culture of populism and class warfare, each shift detonates anger and 'gives you the next Donald Trump'. Ajay argues great societies are 'more Gandhiji and less Karl Marx': they absorb change together.
core_ideas.quote: And when Karl Marx wrote that the history of the world is a history of class warfare, it's not a fair description of the world as it is. It is a fair description of the world as he sought to make it.

core_ideas.concept: Saving the X Industry and the Truth About Tariffs
core_ideas.explanation: Propping up a favoured industry, whether jute, local producers or anything 'ours', is paid for by other industries whose losses go unseen. Tariffs protect a small group of producers at the expense of your own people, a transfer from poor consumers to rich interest groups. Ajay notes that China runs the same industrial-policy playbook as India, 'just done 5x more extreme'.
core_ideas.quote: Tariffs always harm your own people. You think you're protecting a small bunch of producers, you're harming your own people.

core_ideas.explanation: Price controls always cause scarcity, and rent is no exception. Landlords stop maintaining buildings, which is why Marine Drive has sprawling flats renting for a few hundred rupees in dilapidated buildings. Developers stop building, and tenants stop economising on space. It sounds compassionate, but it shrinks the supply of affordable housing for those who need it most. Amit sees this as the danger in Zohran Mamdani's New York platform.
core_ideas.quote: Why are those buildings old and dilapidated? Because the owner doesn't have an incentive to look after them, he's not making any money from them.

core_ideas.explanation: From Hernando de Soto: without formal title, land that people effectively own cannot be borrowed against or confidently improved, so it is 'dead capital'. Giving slum dwellers and long-settled tribals property rights unlocks investment. Rent control does the reverse, killing capital that was alive.
core_ideas.quote: When I think of rent control, I think that what you have just done is that you have taken an apartment or a building or a building block or a neighborhood and you made it dead capital. It is equal to theft.

core_ideas.explanation: Schemes like rent control and price controls let people project virtue. Without the intellectual rigour to trace outcomes, they hurt the poor. Compassion is measured by results, not intentions.
core_ideas.quote: And therefore the truly compassionate people are those who think of the outcomes and they ask the question that are you actually helping the people you're trying to help or are you hurting them?

core_ideas.concept: Reframe the Claim From the Other Side
core_ideas.explanation: Bad policy hides in good-sounding words. Hazlitt pairs them: more credit means more debt. Higher farm prices mean dearer food for city workers. Subsidies mean higher taxes. More exports ultimately means more imports. Higher wage rates mean higher costs of production. Restating a claim from the opposite side reveals what is really being proposed.
core_ideas.quote: When they say that the way to economic salvation is to increase credit, it is just as if they said that the way to economic salvation is to increase debt.

core_ideas.explanation: Talk of 'the nation' or 'the good of society' can hide who actually gains and who loses. Ask what happens to real people.
core_ideas.quote: Many of the most frequent fallacies in economic reasoning come from the propensity, especially marked today, to think in terms of an abstraction, the collectivity, the nation, and to forget or ignore the individuals who make it up and give it meaning.

core_ideas.concept: The Hidden Immorality of Cost-Benefit Analysis
core_ideas.explanation: Via Suyash Rai: aggregate cost-benefit sums hide that one group bears real costs now while another enjoys benefits that are often imagined and in the future. Demonetisation, in Amit's view, had costs and no benefits at all.
core_ideas.quote: They often don't realize that the cost is on one group of people, the benefit is on another group of people. And there is an inherent immorality on this.

core_ideas.explanation: Five lenses for judging any policy. First, opportunity cost: what is the unseen alternative, and whose money is being taken? Second, general welfare over interest-group welfare. Third, incentives and distortions. Fourth, the price system as sacred information. Fifth, how capital formation and savings work.
core_ideas.quote: Prices are how we get information about what others can do for us and what we could possibly do for them.

core_ideas.explanation: Hazlitt quotes Adam Smith: what is prudence in a family can scarcely be folly in a kingdom. Amit extends it. In personal life decent people are libertarian: we don't force friends what to eat or steal to pay for our meal. Yet one level of abstraction up, at the level of the state, coercion and social engineering suddenly seem fine. The task is to reconcile our personal values with how we think about the state.
core_ideas.quote: All decent people, in our personal dealings, we are libertarian.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: When Amit mentions a secret project, Ajay warns him: 'the FSB, they scrape YouTube, they will hear the words. Secret project. And now they will start tapping your phone.' Then he helpfully explains that the FSB is the new name of the KGB.
After Ajay's paragliding confession, Amit asks: 'Are you the first economist to puke on a forest?' Then he follows up: 'If you puke on a forest but nobody sees it, did you puke?'

Amit reads Hazlitt's swipe at an unnamed 'brilliant economist' whose flippant line was 'In the long run we are all dead', and asks Ajay to guess which of his heroes it is. Ajay: 'I love John Maynard Keynes dearly and one of his crimes was that he was wise, witty, and wonderful.' Amit: 'That was the only thing that was not a crime.' Amit then twists the line: in the long run, 'we are wrong'.
Amit explains that intuition tells us the world must be controlled from the top down, then notices Ajay smiling: 'Because you are the man on the top controlling.'

Amit says the show is 'constantly throwing light bulbs at the screen', not literally. Ajay then pitches Everything is Everything merch: a cannon beside the TV that fires defunct tungsten bulbs at the viewer, with Amit controlling the timing from inside the show.

The running Bengali-economist gag. In Bastiat's parable, the man who says the broken window is good for the economy is 'no doubt a wise Bengali economist'. Amit later explains: 'I am a Bengali. The name doesn't indicate it... he doesn't like Bengali economists in particular, and I don't like Bengali economists either.' He then adds that 'a certain Gujarati hubris' also comes into play sometimes.

Ajay on India paying a foreign company to launch an Indian astronaut: it's cheaper than doing it through ISRO, with the same propaganda value. Taken to its logical conclusion, 'what you need is an AI video'.
Amit on conspiracy theories that the moon landings happened in Nevada: 'which of course they did not, they happened on the moon. We are fairly certain of that.'

In the jute story, Amit slips in a Hindi pun on jute and 'jhoot' (lie), the 'Jute ka Jhoot' of the chapter title, and refuses to explain it. Ajay gets it 'forty-five milliseconds later'. Amit then says the jute fixation gets his goat, adding: 'I should be careful about what I say because I don't have a goat.'
Amit's T-shirt line for the show's merch: 'Make trade not war.' He follows up by asking whether Ajay prefers making trade or making love. The answer: 'Unprintable.'

Amit stumbles over Arthur C. Clarke's line, 'any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic'. He calls 'indistinguishable' 'as difficult a word as internationalization' and says it as 'internationalization from magic'. He decides that if you turned a chicken into an EV in front of Clarke, 'he would say why this is magic.'

Ajay defends Zohran Mamdani with the old saw: 'He who is not a communist when he is young has no heart. He who is a communist as an adult has no brain. So give him a break.' Amit: 'Thirty-four is old enough.'

Amit says Ajay's mentee is 'turning into an Ajay, which is rather alarming', and asks how Ajay feels about young Ajays running around the world. Ajay: they'll soon get over the delusion that 'there is anything here which is somehow special.' Amit: 'Oh my god, such modesty.'

Gunnar Myrdal, the Nobel-winning economist who argued that machinery was good for the West but not for India because demand for labour might fall. Amit's verdict: 'Dude wins the Nobel Prize for talking this shit.'

George Santayana, The Life of Reason (1905), quoted in Hazlitt's book too: 'Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.' Amit invokes it against every new wave of technophobia, from the Luddites to AI.

Adam Smith's pin makers, via Hazlitt: one unaided workman could scarcely make one pin a day, while with machinery he could make 4,800. By Luddite logic the pin industry should already have had 99.98% unemployment.
Ajay recalls the old line about bank robbers in the American West, 'Why do you rob banks? Because that's where the money is', to explain why governments everywhere raid the financial system.
Margaret Thatcher's 'don't speak to me of society, there are individuals', invoked by Amit along with 'the smallest minority is the individual'.
James C. Scott in Seeing Like a State, quoted by Ajay: 'The greatest fertilizer of all is the tender gaze of an owner.'

Zohran Mamdani, winner of New York's Democratic mayoral primary and son of filmmaker Mira Nair and academic Mahmood Mamdani. Amit finds him charming and condemns the racist attacks on him, but calls his policies, such as government grocery stores, free buses and rent control, 'a throwback to the worst excesses of the twentieth century'. Amit is a big Mira Nair fan and won't tolerate 'any nonsense' about her.
